walkthroughs.h2: Why the demand curve slopes down
walkthroughs.body_html: When apples cost 50p each, you might buy 10. At £2 each, you buy 2. Higher price discourages buying because of the income effect (you feel poorer) and the substitution effect (you switch to pears). Plot price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis: the curve slopes downward from top-left to bottom-right.

walkthroughs.h2: Why the supply curve slopes up
walkthroughs.body_html: Producers want profit. At £2 an apple, more farmers plant orchards because revenue covers costs. At 10p, only the most efficient bother. So higher price = higher quantity supplied. The supply curve slopes upward from bottom-left to top-right.

Where the demand and supply curves cross is the equilibrium. At this price, buyers want exactly what sellers offer — no shortage, no surplus. If price is too high, surplus builds up and price falls. If too low, shortage forms and price rises until balance returns.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: Demand always falls when supply increases.
A change in price shifts the demand curve.
A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
PED measures whether a product is expensive or cheap.

mcqs.q: What does price elasticity of demand measure?
options: PED measures whether a product is expensive or cheap.
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price — the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price.
PED measures how flexible or stretchy a product is.
Demand always falls when supply increases.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
A sustained rise in the general price level over time — reducing the purchasing power of money. Measured by the percentage change in a price index.
Demand always falls when supply increases.
Inflation is when prices are high.
